tldr: A mobile robot was deployed in a harsh subarctic forest over an entire year, thoroughly investigating how seasonal changes—such as 60 °C temperature swings and heavy snowfall—affect the performance and fragility of state-of-the-art SLAM and sensor modalities (lidar, radar, and cameras).
hero_caption: Table showing the relative error against a proprioceptive (odometry) baseline (SARTE) and failure rates of evaluated methods across six distinct navigation routes. Many advanced SLAM methods degrade compared to a simple wheel odometry + IMU baseline, clearly illustrating how added complexity leads to system fragility.
overview:
Autonomous mobile robots hold great potential for automating tasks in forestry, mining, and environmental monitoring across subarctic regions. However, dense tree canopies and snowstorms obstruct GNSS signals, while cloud connectivity is unavailable in these high-latitude forests, making onboard sensing and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) essential. Established SLAM technologies relying on lidars, cameras, and millimeter-wave radars have typically been evaluated in structured urban settings or environments with minimal seasonal changes, leaving their behavior largely unknown under harsh wilderness conditions with multi-meter snowdrifts and 60 °C temperature swings.

To address this, the research team deployed a large unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) in a subarctic boreal forest in Quebec, Canada, conducting field trials over 12 months with a total travel distance of 64 km. They evaluated nine odometry, localization, and mapping methods across seasonal transitions—ranging from a simple proprioceptive baseline using wheel encoders and an IMU to state-of-the-art lidar SLAM, radar SLAM, and deep-learning-based visual SLAM—to thoroughly compare their robustness.

The experimental findings revealed surprising results. Despite operating off-road where severe wheel slip is common, most state-of-the-art SLAM methods were outperformed in accuracy by the simple wheel odometry baseline. Adding complex graph optimization and loop closures made the systems more fragile due to false perceptual matches. Furthermore, in cross-season localization where the robot localizes within a map built during the summer, wide-field lidar exhibited strong resilience, whereas visual and radar methods suffered catastrophic failures due to dramatic appearance and terrain changes caused by snow.
contributions: Collected 64 km of real-world deployment data over one full year in a subarctic boreal forest, comprehensively analyzing the impact of seasonal changes on nine lidar, radar, and visual SLAM/odometry methods.
Systematized a qualitative and quantitative evaluation framework for outdoor robotics to eliminate ambiguity, formalizing concepts of disturbances, stressors, robustness, and fragility.

Quantitatively and visually demonstrated the mechanism where winter snowbanks and terrain flattening bias visual features toward the upper part of images, causing a rapid surge in translational drift.
Demonstrated the fundamental limitations of vision and radar alongside the clear superiority of lidar in cross-season localization tasks using maps built in different seasons.

sections.heading: Why Deploy Autonomous Robots in Subarctic Forests Now?
sections.summary: While demand for autonomous robotics in subarctic forests is rising due to shifting northern activities, GNSS denial and extreme cold pose major barriers. Through a year-long field deployment, this study uncovers the disruptive impact of seasonal variations on state-of-the-art odometry and SLAM techniques.
sections.details:
With changing global climates, industrial interest in resource extraction, forestry, and environmental monitoring in subarctic regions has grown rapidly. However, operating in these frigid, high-latitude environments is exhausting and dangerous for humans due to short daylight hours and long, grueling winters. While UGVs are strongly desired for automation, autonomous driving technology faces a triple penalty in this setting.

First, satellite navigation (GNSS) is unreliable. At high latitudes, satellite elevation angles are low, signals are obstructed by dense evergreen canopies, and antenna icing and atmospheric attenuation further degrade reception. Second, cellular and satellite communications are unavailable, preventing robots from offloading heavy computation to the cloud and requiring full onboard autonomy. Third, battery capacities plummet at low temperatures while energy consumption spikes on soft snow and muddy terrain.

Most challenging of all are the dramatic seasonal changes. Temperature swings exceed 60 °C between summer and winter, and several meters of snow accumulate during winter. Trees are blanketed in snow, and uneven ground features are completely buried beneath a flat white expanse. In this study, nine odometry and SLAM configurations were evaluated over a year in this boreal forest, rigorously exposing the link between algorithmic complexity and real-world system fragility.

sections.heading: Leaving Paved Urban Streets Behind for Multi-Season Fields
sections.summary: Existing SLAM benchmarks are heavily biased toward urban areas and temperate climates, with very few studies tackling seasonal transitions. This section introduces the Köppen climate classification to organize prior research and outline how natural seasonal shifts affect lidars, radars, and cameras.
sections.details:
Outdoor robotics environments have historically been lumped into broad "on-road" and "off-road" categories. However, the authors argue for a clear distinction between "off-pavement" paths—which still retain visual and structural trail cues like dirt roads—and true "off-trail" environments, where paths do not exist and vehicles must traverse raw vegetation and obstacles.

To fairly compare long-term experiments worldwide, the paper adopts the Köppen-Geiger climate classification. Many multi-season datasets (such as Oxford RobotCar or 4Seasons) were collected in urban settings subject to municipal interventions like snow clearing and street lighting. In contrast, fewer than 8% of field robotics studies investigate multi-season natural environments, and most of those remain confined to temperate zones (Cfa or Csa) where vegetation changes dominate.

In cold, wet subarctic regions (Dfc), seasonal changes go far beyond appearance: heavy snowfall alters the physical volume of the ground. This raises the robot's ride height and alters vehicle pitch and roll across seasons, shifting the sensors' field of view. Cameras suffer from intense snow glare, dynamic range saturation, and under-exposure. 2D millimeter-wave radars fall victim to ground strikes caused by vehicle tilt. For lidars, rather than falling snowflakes themselves, structural terrain changes such as several-meter-high snowbanks present the most critical obstacle.

sections.heading: How to Measure Algorithmic "Fragility" in Hostile Environments?
sections.summary: To assess real-world field repeatability rather than laboratory reproducibility, a taxonomy based on disturbances and stressors is established. A new evaluation metric, SARTE, is also introduced to benchmark drift when ground-truth orientation is unavailable.
sections.details:
Unlike controlled laboratory experiments that systematically vary single parameters, harsh field trials expose systems to multiple, unpredictable challenges simultaneously. The paper imports terminology from continuum mechanics to clarify evaluation concepts for robotics:

- Disturbance: Sudden, short-duration events, such as wheel slippage or collisions with trees and rocks.
- Stressor: Sustained environmental conditions that put prolonged strain on the system, such as continuous deep snow cover or extreme cold.
- Robustness: Sub-linear error growth over time as stress and disturbances are applied.
- Fragility: Super-linear error growth under stress, leading to breakdown. Systems that fail abruptly without warning are termed "brittle."

Algorithms are categorized into four complexity tiers: proprioceptive (wheel encoders + IMU), standalone exteroceptive odometry, exteroceptive methods with loop closing (PGO), and prior-map-based localization, allowing researchers to evaluate whether increased algorithmic complexity truly yields greater robustness.

Furthermore, external optical motion capture cannot be deployed in vast forests. While differential GNSS (PPK) provides accurate position fixes, collecting independent, high-accuracy 3D orientation ground truth (GT) under dense canopy is challenging. To address this, the authors introduce SARTE, a sliding-window rigid alignment metric that measures local positional drift while eliminating heading ambiguity, even without orientation GT. They also formalize Failure Rate (runs terminated prematurely) and Localization Failure Rate (LFR, the fraction of distance traversed while lost).

sections.heading: A 500-kg Mobile Robot and Six Diverse Navigation Routes
sections.summary: A 500-kg UGV equipped with lidar, radar, stereo cameras, GNSS, and an IMU logged 64 km of data across six routes spanning paved paths to rugged off-trail wilderness over one year. Nine established open-source methods were selected for benchmarking.
sections.details:
The test platform was a Clearpath Warthog UGV weighing approximately 0.5 tons. During winter (January to March), it was retrofitted with tracks to maintain mobility in deep snow. Its sensor suite included a 128-beam RoboSense Ruby Plus lidar, a Navtech 360-degree 2D millimeter-wave radar, a ZED X stereo camera, multiple GNSS receivers, and a VectorNav IMU.

Six courses with distinct environmental difficulties were established:
- Red (~300 m): A flat, paved semi-urban loop, serving as the simplest baseline.
- Blue (~500 m): Leaves paved roads, descends a steep forest slope, and pushes through deep snowbanks to return in winter.
- Green (~500 m): Rugged off-trail terrain with steep elevation changes and dense brush that completely occludes camera views.
- Orange (~2200 m): The longest route, combining gravel forest roads with an open quarry.
- Yellow (~1900 m): A long dirt-road and off-road trail containing multiple loops.
- Magenta (~700 m): An off-trail route threading through a quarry with frequent vehicle contact against boulders and brush.

These tracks were driven across all four seasons. In total, nine open-source pipelines (spanning 11 odometry and SLAM configurations) were tested offline: lidar-based (KISS-ICP/SLAM, 2Fast-2Lamaa, WILN), radar-based (RT&R, Navtech-Radar-SLAM/ORORA), vision-based (ORB-SLAM3, cuVSLAM, DROID-SLAM), and the proprioceptive baseline (wheel encoders + IMU).

sections.heading: Shocking Results: Can SOTA SLAM Lose to Wheel Odometry?
sections.summary: Experiments revealed that most exteroceptive SLAM algorithms exhibited larger errors than basic wheel odometry and suffered catastrophic failures from false loop closures. Snow-induced lack of ground texture was also shown to cripple visual SLAM accuracy.
sections.details:
The experimental results challenged conventional assumptions.

In standalone odometry benchmarks, the proprioceptive baseline combining wheel encoders and IMU achieved an average SARTE of 3.6% across all routes—a remarkably strong performance despite severe wheel slippage on off-road terrain. In contrast, exteroceptive odometry methods averaged 10 percentage points worse than this baseline. Lidar methods were the only ones to consistently outperform proprioception (with KISS-ICP achieving an average error below 1%), whereas radar and visual pipelines suffered from heavy drift and tracking dropouts.

Even more severe was the failure of loop closure via pose graph optimization (PGO). While revisiting known areas and optimizing trajectories should theoretically improve accuracy, the repetitive visual appearance of trees in subarctic forests led place recognition algorithms to trigger frequent false-positive loop closures. Navtech-Radar-SLAM was hit hardest: ScanContext registered 9,860 incorrect loop closures, causing graph optimization to severely distort trajectories and inflating errors by 75 percentage points.

Visual SLAM algorithms (ORB-SLAM3, cuVSLAM, DROID-SLAM) were exceptionally fragile to seasonal changes. In summer, keypoints were evenly distributed across images. In winter, uniform snow cover wiped out all visual features from the bottom half of frames (the ground plane), clustering them exclusively along the distant upper canopy. Relying solely on distant tree branches while losing proximal ground points degraded translational scale estimation, driving errors above 30%.

Finally, during cross-season localization—localizing in winter using summer maps—lidar pipelines utilizing local voxel submaps (such as 2Fast-2Lamaa) tracked successfully. Conversely, radar and visual methods found virtually no matching features across seasons, frequently losing localization immediately after starting and failing to recover.

sections.heading: Hard-Won Lessons from Real-World Cold-Weather Field Operations
sections.summary: Thirty-five days of field deployments highlighted mobility differences across snow conditions, hardware breakdowns from 60 °C temperature swings, and sensor calibration hurdles. Practical engineering solutions to snowbank occlusions are also detailed.
sections.details:
Beyond algorithmic metrics, the paper details raw operational challenges and the practical insights gained:

- Snow Quality Dictates Mobility: In light, powdery November snow, tracks easily navigated 40-cm depths. However, in wet, heavy April spring snow of the same depth, tracks dug out snow from underneath the vehicle, high-centering the chassis and causing complete wheel slip. The team had to recover the stuck UGV 62 times throughout the year.
- Extreme Temperatures and Hardware Failures: Diurnal temperature variations reached up to 26 °C in a single day (-1 °C to 25 °C). High mechanical vibrations under extreme cold led to three catastrophic failures where Li-ion battery modules cracked and disconnected. At -25 °C, stereo cameras experienced auto-exposure malfunctions, outputting completely blown-out, over-exposed white frames.
- Six-DOF Calibration with Industrial Cranes: Off-road driving induces aggressive roll and pitch variations, requiring precise IMU-camera extrinsic calibration. However, manually tilting a 500-kg machine is impossible. The authors solved this by lifting the vehicle with an industrial crane and swaying it in mid-air.
- Snowbank Occlusions After Plowing: Snow plows created roadside snowbanks up to 3 meters tall. These drastically altered the environment compared to summer teach runs, causing lidar SLAM to fail. The team engineered a pragmatic fix: filtering out all lidar points below 1.5 m from the sensor (2.6 m above ground) to force the pipeline to match against elevated tree canopies, successfully restoring repeat tracking.

sections.heading: Questioning Lab Assumptions to Conquer the Real Wilderness
sections.summary: One year of trials proved that complex state-of-the-art SLAM is not inherently robust in natural environments. While lidar remains the most reliable sensor, vision and radar face steep challenges. Crucial guidelines for future field robotics research are outlined.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated the fragility of advanced SLAM techniques, engineered primarily for urban or static settings, when deployed in dynamic subarctic nature. The finding that basic proprioceptive sensing (wheel speed + IMU) serves as such a strong baseline, while sophisticated loop closing can trigger system-wide collapse through false matches, offers an important reality check for field roboticists.

The authors recommend three best practices for future field robotics research:
1. Always benchmark against a proprioceptive odometry baseline to justify exteroceptive sensor claims.
2. Report the Köppen-Geiger climate classification to make environmental severity comparable across research groups.
3. Report system Failure Rates alongside average trajectory errors, rather than discarding failed runs from final metrics.

Achieving true autonomy in harsh wilderness requires moving beyond single-season accuracy competitions. Future work must focus on multi-season place recognition and the joint integration of vehicle-terrain interaction dynamics into state estimation.

sections.heading: Visualizing Trajectory Breakdowns Across Real Seasons
sections.summary: The appendix provides qualitative comparisons of estimated trajectories across seasons, visually illustrating scale collapse from snowbanks and catastrophic trajectory distortion caused by false radar loop closures.
sections.details:
The appendix presents raw estimated trajectory visualizations for the Orange, Yellow, and Magenta courses.

While the lidar-based WILN pipeline demonstrated high accuracy, it lost lateral constraints on a straight section of the winter Yellow course bounded by massive snowbanks, visibly drifting away from ground truth. KISS-SLAM, which incorporates loop closures into KISS-ICP, improved scale estimation on summer runs but introduced incorrect rotational constraints that skewed the overall trajectory heading.

The most dramatic failure appeared in Navtech-Radar-SLAM. Along uniform stretches of dirt road where tree geometry was repetitive, it matched locations hundreds of meters apart as the same place. As a result, graph optimization severely warped a straight road into an artificial circular loop. The deep-learning-based DROID-SLAM also lost scale tracking in autumn and winter due to feature scarcity, falsely estimating traversed distances to be multiples of actual vehicle movement.

takeaways: "More complex SLAM equals higher accuracy" does not hold in harsh wilderness; false loop closures are catastrophic, making simple odometry safer in natural environments.
Proprioceptive odometry (wheels + IMU) is an exceptionally strong baseline even on rough terrain and should always be included as a benchmark.
Uniform snow cover pushes visual features into the distant upper canopy, causing severe translational scale drift in standalone cameras.
For multi-season localization, 3D lidar with a wide vertical field of view that matches high, unburied structures (like tree canopies) is currently the most dependable approach.
limitations: While high-accuracy positioning ground truth was gathered, orientation ground truth (pitch/roll/yaw) under dense forest canopies remains difficult to acquire independently, complicating separate rotational error evaluations.
All tests were conducted on a single large skid-steer vehicle (Warthog), leaving the dynamics of different chassis designs, wheel configurations, and vehicle sizes unexplored.
While summer, autumn, and winter data are extensive, data from the spring thaw period is limited, constraining the evaluation of vehicle performance in deep mud and slush.
